chunks: "A pull-up or pull-down resistor ties a signal to the supply or to ground through a resistor, so that the line has a known default state when nothing is driving it.
If a CMOS input is left floating, it's high impedance, so it picks up noise, can sit at a mid-level, and can oscillate or even draw extra current.
A pull-up gives it a default high; a pull-down gives it a default low.
When something does drive it, a switch, or a driver, that overrides the resistor, because the resistor is deliberately weak.
They're also needed for open-drain outputs, like I2C, which can only pull the line low. The resistor is what pulls it high again. To spec one, I look at the two sides.

The resistor has to be small enough that the node rises fast enough, which is the RC of the resistor and the node capacitance, and that leakage doesn't pull the level down, so leakage times R stays small compared to the noise margin.

It has to be big enough that when the line is pulled low, the current V over R is acceptable for the driver and the power budget, so for I2C it can't exceed the sink rating, about 3 milliamps, which gives about a kilohm at 3.
3 volts. A typical default is 10 kilohms for slow control signals, 4. 7 kilohms for I2C at 100 or 400 kilohertz, and 100 kilohms or more for low-power or gate pull-downs."
